stage_3_narrative.description: This watercolor depicts a plantation scene in the American South, dated c. 1785–1795, attributed to John Rose. The composition presents a horizontal frieze-like arrangement of thirteen figures of African descent distributed across the foreground in a shallow spatial plane. Two substantial rectangular buildings with pitched roofs frame the composition on the left and right; a row of smaller structures (worker cabins or cabaña) recedes into the middle distance, accompanied by trees and a water feature with small boats. The scene is organized as a documentary tableau of simultaneous activities: in the center foreground, four figures (fig_06, fig_07, fig_08, fig_09) are bent forward holding long-handled implements (azada or hoe-like tools), their postures consistent with agricultural labor. On the right foreground, two figures (fig_12, fig_13) stand upright holding stringed instruments (banjo or similar gourd-bodied instruments), with earthenware vessels (olla or tinaja) positioned at their feet. The remaining figures (fig_01, fig_02, fig_03, fig_04, fig_05, fig_10, fig_11) are distributed across the left and center foreground in upright standing postures, their bodies oriented toward the central activity or toward each other, suggesting observation, conversation, or waiting. All figures wear head wraps (tocado) in white linen or cotton, with the exception of fig_11, who wears a black brimmed hat (sombrero). Upper garments are predominantly blue (camiseta), with lower garments in white, orange, yellow, or orange-red tones (saya). Most figures are depicted with bare feet (descalzo). The lighting is diffuse and even, with warm golden-brown tones dominating the architecture and ground, and soft shadows suggesting overcast daylight or sheltered conditions. The color palette emphasizes earth tones (ochre, tan, beige) with accents of blue, orange, red, yellow, and green in garments; white head wraps and garments provide visual contrast against the dark skin tones rendered consistently throughout. The scene type is a secular, documentary costumbrismo composition depicting plantation life and the material culture of enslaved and free Afrodescendants in the late 18th-century Americas. The specific iconographic type is a plantation labor and leisure scene, combining visual documentation of work (agricultural labor with tools) and music-making (stringed instruments), organized as a composite tableau rather than a narrative sequence. No religious iconography, allegorical elements, or casta-painting hierarchies are present. The composition does not depict an individual portrait but rather a collective scene of communal activity. The provenance is listed as a plantation in present-day Beaufort County, South Carolina, consistent with the visual evidence of plantation architecture and the documented presence of enslaved Africans in the Lowcountry during this period.
